messages.subject_clean: Virtual identical latent variables can't be merged/fixed to 1?
messages.body_plain:
Hey all

In my following model I apply fixed-links modelling in order to dissociate different sources of variance within two elementary cognitive tasks (ECTs).
For each ECT, I model a constant process (processes common to all task levels, not changing across levels, e.g. basal speed processes) and a variable process (processes increasing across task levels, e.g. increasing complexity).

I specify the following model according to my theoretical assumptions:
hick = variable with increasing complexity (factor loadings fixed to 1, 2, and 4)
cHICK = constant variable (factor loadings fixed to 1)
similar fixing for cpt
+ restraints by setting covariances to 0 in order to assume independent latent variables

modelA      <- 'hick   =~ 1*hick_rt1m   + 2*hick_rt2m   + 4*hick_rt3m
                  cHICK =~ 1*hick_rt1m   + 1*hick_rt2m   + 1*hick_rt3m
                  cCPT =~  1*cpt_rt1m + 1*cpt_rt2m + 1*cpt_rt3m
                  cpt =~ 0.25*cpt_rt1m + 2*cpt_rt2m + 3*cpt_rt3m
                  hick ~~ cpt
                  hick ~~ 0*cHICK
                  cpt ~~ 0*cCPT
                  hick ~~ 0*cCPT
                  cpt ~~ 0*cHICK
                  cHICK ~~ cCPT'

This model fits well / good indices (p = .31) -> graph on the left
due to the standardized coefficients I can assume that the two constant processes represent virtual identical processes (cHICK and cCPT = .975). Anyhow, when I model the same model with the two constant variables as one variable (-> graph on the right), then the model won't fit anymore (p = .004) and show rather poor indices.
(Modindices tell me that the (new) constant variable should be covaried with hick...)

can anyone tell me, from a methodological perspective, why it works for the two contant model and why it doesn't work at all for the one constant model?
To my understanding, the model on the right is more parsimonious and should be better than the model on the left...

messages.subject: Potential Bug in Modification Indices (in the current version, 0.5-18)
messages.subject_clean: Potential Bug in Modification Indices (in the current version, 0.5-18)
messages.body_plain:
In a model in which two groups are specified and some parameters are constrained to be equal across groups, modification indices behave differently in the new (0.5-18) and in the previous (0.5-17) versions of lavaan.
Version 0.5-17: the indices take the exact same value for the same parameters in group 1 and in group 2. Although I am not an expert, this makes a lot of sense to me.
Version 0.5-18: the values of the modification indices are different among groups.
Below you can find a toy example that shows the issue. Please try it with the latest version of lavaan and with the older version if you want to see it yourself.

I think that this might be a bug

######################################################################################################
# install version 0.5-17
install.packages("http://cran.r-project.org/src/contrib/Archive/lavaan/lavaan_0.5-17.tar.gz", repo = NULL, type = "source")
# install latest version
#install.packages("lavaan")
library(lavaan)
library(MASS)

# simulate the data for two groups
set.seed(1)
cormat1 <- cormat2 <-  matrix(.4, nrow = 4, ncol = 4)
diag(cormat1) <- diag(cormat2) <- 1
cormat2[1,2] <- cormat2[2,1] <- .1 # introduce a clear difference among the groups

data1 <- mvrnorm(n = 100,
                 mu = c(1, 1, 1, 1),
                 Sigma = cormat1)
data2 <- mvrnorm(n = 100,
                 mu = c(1, 1, 1, 1),
                 Sigma = cormat2)
data <- data.frame(rbind(data1, data2))
data$group <- c(rep(1, 100), rep(2, 100))

# define a toy moel, in which the covariances are
# constrained to be equal
model <- '
X1 ~~ c(a1, a1)*X2 + c(a2, a2)*X3 + c(a3, a3)*X4
X2 ~~ c(a4, a4)*X3 + c(a5, a5)*X4
X3 ~~ c(a6, a6)*X4
X1 ~~ a7*X1
X2 ~~ a8*X2
X3 ~~ a9*X3
X4 ~~ a9*X4'

# fit the model with lavaan
fit1 <- sem(model = model, data = data, group = "group",
    meanstructure = FALSE)

modindices(fit1)
########################################################################################################

messages.subject_clean: Scaling by fixed loading and fixed latent variance
messages.body_plain:
Dear Lavaan users,

I have some confusion with the scaling method. In the model that I am working with, I have three latent variables, each of which has three indicators.

There are several ways that we can set the scale of the latent variable. By default, cfa() would fix the factor loading of the first indicator of each latent variable to 1. Like in the following example:

model<-'

updating =~ Task1 + Task4 + Task6

inhibition =~ Task9 + Task7 + Task3

shifting =~ Task2 + Task5 + Task8

'

fit.model.m <- cfa(model,estimator = "mlm",data = EF.data.M)

This model works fine.

Alternatively, we can set the variance of each latent variable to 1, this could be done by adding an input argument. So I did the following:

fit.model.alt.m <- cfa(model,estimator = "mlm",data = EF.data.M,std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE)

However, this time I am getting a warning message that covariance matrix of latent variable is not positive definite.

Another alternative is to specify the fixed latent variance in the model, so I did the following:

model.std.lv <http://model.std.lv><-'

updating =~ NA*Task1 + Task4 + Task6

inhibition =~ NA*Task9 + Task7 + Task3

shifting =~ NA*Task2 + Task5 + Task8

updating ~~ 1*updating

inhibition ~~ 1*inhibition

shifting ~~ 1*shifting

'

fit.model.std.lv.m <- cfa(model.std.lv <http://model.std.lv>,estimator = "mlm",data = EF.data.M)

This time, I am having the same warning message that covariance matrix of latent variable is not positive definite.

I thought that the above three ways were equivalent, so I couldn't understand why they might lead to different results. Do you have any ideas why this is the case? Or am I making some mistakes with the models?

Many thanks in advance,

Beinan

This is by design. It is simply a different way to compute the MIs when
they are constrained. Think of it this way: if you have two parameters
(say, A and B) constrained to be equal, and you want a MI for A and for
B, there are two ways:

- release both of them at the same time; this gives the same MI for both
A and B, and is what is done in 0.5-17

- release only A (or B), while the other parameter remains at the same
value: this is what is done in 0.5-18

What is missing (for now) in 0.5-18 is another function that will allow
you the check the MIs when an equality constraint is released; this
affects all other values too, and a new function for doing just that is
under construction and will be available soon (in dev 0.5-19).

The motivation for this change is to get more consistent behavior when
arbitrary constraints (not only simple equality constraints) have been
used when estimating the model.

Yves.

When the estimator = WLSMV, the anova() function (which just calls the

covariance/mean level.

Are the factors correlated or orthogonal?  If orthogonal, and if all terms are standardized, and if the model fits in an absolute or chi-square sense, then the sum of squared Loadings, factor by factor, will approximate the corresponding eigenvalue. messages.body_plain:
If “correlations” means you have the correlation matrix of the observed variables, then certainly you can calculate eigenvalues.  If “correlations” means correlations among the factors, then I would have to work that out a bit more.

--Ed Rigdon

Sent: Monday, May 11, 2015 4:12 PM
To: lav...@googlegroups.com
Subject: Re: how to compute eigen from factor loadings?

Hello Ed,

the reported factors loadings are oblique (Promax). I have also the means and correlation matrix. Nothing about chi-square fit, nothing else.

So, is it possible to compute exactly the eigen values having these information?

Thank you for your advice and recommended book!

On Saturday, May 9, 2015 at 5:36:40 PM UTC+3, Edward Rigdon wrote:
>
> Are the factors correlated or orthogonal?  If orthogonal, and if all terms are standardized, and if the model fits in an absolute or chi-square sense, then the sum of squared Loadings, factor by factor, will approximate the corresponding eigenvalue.  But if the factors covary, then there is no one-to-one correspondence between factors and eigenvalues.  Either way, though, this will only be an approximation to what you would get if you had the covariance matrix itself.

Hello Anna,

I think you haven't defined right your configural3 model. It should be either

f1 =~ c(a1,a1)*item1 + item2 + item3 + item4 +item5 + item6 + item7 + item8 + item9 +item10 + item11 + item12 + item13 + item 14 + item15 + item16 + item17 + item18 + item19 + item20
.... (the rest commands are ok)
f1 ~~ c(1, NA)*f1
....

or

f1 =~ c(1,1)*item1 + item2 + item3 + item4 +item5 + item6 + item7 + item8 + item9 +item10 + item11 + item12 + item13 + item 14 + item15 + item16 + item17 + item18 + item19 + item20
.... (the rest commands are ok)
f1 ~~ f1 (# both factor variances are free to be estimated)
....

this way, you define the same scale for f1 in both groups and cross-group comparisons are meaningful. The way you wrote configural3 determines a different scale of f1 in each group.

The models that are compared with the commands you mention should be nested, models that are fitted does not mean that they can be compared.

Also models with the same degrees of freedom are not necessarily equivalent.

Best regards,

Myrto

messages.body_plain:
On 05/15/2015 11:19 PM, Lucas Damian Gorné wrote:
> Hello,
> I have read that in order to estimate standar errors and test the model
> the data set must be transformed according to the Cholensky
> factorization transformation. Does function sem make these
> transformation when se="bootstrap" and test="bootstrap"?

Only if test = "bootstrap". In that case, we use a model-based bootstrap
(often referred to as the Bollen-Stine bootstrap), since we need to draw
bootstrap samples under the null. To do that, we need to transform the
data so that it aligns with the null hypothesis (that the model fits).
To do this,  we need to take the 'square root' of the model-implied
Sigma. This can be done using a Cholesky factorization, but lavaan uses
an eigen decomposition, inside the function lav_matrix_symmetric_sqrt()

See the file

https://github.com/yrosseel/lavaan/blob/master/R/lav_bootstrap_lrt.R

around the lines 74 - 92.

Yves.

messages.body_plain:
On 05/10/2015 06:58 PM, kmarkus via lavaan wrote:
> Are chi-square difference/likelihood ratio tests considered valid for
> pairs of models that differ in dimensionality?  I was under the
> impression that models with reduced dimensionality in terms of the
> variables (as distinct from dimensionality in terms of parameters)
> constitute boundary solutions that can impact the validity of such
> statistics for model comparison.

It is often possible to reparameterize a one-dimensional model as a
two-dimensional model by adding all sorts of constraints. If this is
possible, the one-dimensional model is nested within the two-dimensional
model. Not in the strict 'parameter' sense, but in the more general
covariance/mean structure sense. See also

Bentler, P. M., & Satorra, A. (2010). Testing model nesting and
equivalence. _Psychological Methods, 15_, 111-123.     doi:10.1037/a0019625

In this case (ie, models are nested in the general covariance/mean
structure sense), the regular chi-square difference test is still valid.

This is also true for the *scaled* chi-square difference test if you use
either the method described in Satorra & Bentler (2001), or the method
described in Satorra & Bentler (2010), but NOT if you use the method
described in Satorra (2000). The latter requires that the models are
nested in the strict parameter sense.

      Satorra, A. (2000). Scaled and adjusted restricted tests in
      multi-sample analysis of moment structures. In Heijmans, R.D.H.,
      Pollock, D.S.G. & Satorra, A. (eds.), Innovations in multivariate
      statistical analysis. A Festschrift for Heinz Neudecker
      (pp.233-247). London: Kluwer Academic Publishers.

      Satorra, A., & Bentler, P. M. (2001). A scaled difference
      chi-square test statistic for moment structure analysis.
      Psychometrika, 66(4), 507-514.

      Satorra, A., & Bentler, P. M. (2010). Ensuring postiveness of the
      scaled difference chi-square test statistic. Psychometrika, 75(2),
      243-248.

Yves.

But you have just fitted the strong invariance model. The "residuals"
are not included in group.equal=, so the residuals will be freely
estimated in the second group.

parameterizationm, and add "residuals" to the group.equal= argument.
Then, the residuals will be constrained to be equal across groups. But
they will all take on the value of the first/reference group, and this
is 1.0!

Yves.

On 05/20/2015 12:45 AM, ac...@umich.edu wrote:
> Were you able to fit an ALT model at all? I keep on having a problem

> treated differently from the later time points.

I have fitted several ALT models without any issues. But I recommend to
use the lavaan() function for this, and avoid the growth() function. The
latter is only for simple growth models.

Below is an example from a book chapter written by Curran & Bollen (2001).

Yves.

# example from Curran & Bollen (2001) book chapter `The Best of
# Two Worlds'

# note the negative variance for the slope factor.
# this was easy to miss using EQS, since it forces variances
# to be strictly positive...

lower <- '
  2.926
  1.390 4.257
  1.698 2.781 4.536
  1.628 2.437 2.979 5.605
  1.240 0.789 0.903 1.278 3.208
  0.592 1.890 1.419 1.004 1.706 3.994
  0.929 1.278 1.900 1.000 1.567 1.654 3.583
  0.659 0.949 1.731 2.420 0.988 1.170 1.146 3.649 '

COV <- getCov(lower, names=c("anti1", "anti2", "anti3", "anti4",
                              "dep1", "dep2", "dep3", "dep4"))

MEANS <- c(1.750, 1.928, 1.978, 2.322, 2.178, 2.489, 2.294, 2.222)

model <- '
   # growth curve
   i =~ anti1 + 1*anti2 + 1*anti3 + 1*anti4
   i ~ 1; i ~~ i
   s= ~ anti1 + 1*anti2 + 2*anti3 + 3*anti4
   s ~ 1; s ~~ s
   anti1 ~~ anti1
   anti2 ~~ anti2
   anti3 ~~ anti3
   anti4 ~~ anti4

   # autoregressive components
   anti2 ~ a1*anti1
   anti3 ~ a2*anti2
   anti4 ~ a3*anti3
'
fit <- lavaan(model, sample.cov = COV, sample.mean = MEANS,
               sample.nobs = 180, mimic = "EQS")
summary(fit, fit.measures = TRUE)

On 05/19/2015 07:24 PM, NewInMediation wrote:

>
> How can I know ab and total for each group when I try mediation in
> lavaan with groups? I only see one ab and total in the bottom when I
> have two groups and different numbers for two groups.

You need to use a different set of labels for each group. See:

http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/groups.html

So if you have a simple mediation setup as in

m ~ x
y ~ x + m

then you will need to label them as follows (assuming two groups):

m ~ c(a1,a2)*x
y ~ c(c1,c2)*x + c(b1,b2)*m

and the you can define the indirect/total effects for each group as

ab1 := a1*b1
ab2 := a2*b2

total1 := c1 + (a1*b1)
total2 := c2 + (a2*b2)

Yves.

messages.body_plain:
hi O.S.

When you correlate two exogenous variables, you get their covariance. When you correlate two endogenous variables, it is the two residual variances that you are correlating, so it is the residual covariance. The exogenous variables are considered not influenced by other variables (although they actually are). The variances of the endogenous variables include roughly two parts, explained and unexplained variance. The explained variances of the endogenous variables are explained by the exogenous variables. The unexplained variances of the endogenous variables are residual (left unexplained) variances. So the covariance between exogenous variables (e.g., observed IV) are theoretically not the same thing as the residual covariance between endogenous variables (e.g., observed DV)

The operator "~" does not mean correlation, but regression. See the detail about operators in lavaan here: http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/syntax1.html

hope this help.

ya

I am working on a report using R / lavaan, while my colleague uses MPlus. Unfortunately, I have some problems replicating her results and get warnings with lavaan, and the results do not match.

My colleague used ML estimation and multiply imputed missing data. I did the same using both Amelia and mice (for comparison).

                B1 B2 B3;

          MISSING = ALL (777);

DATA IMPUTATION:
          IMPUTE = P1 (c) P2 (c) P3 P4 A1 A2 A3 ;
                 NDATASETS = 10;
      TYPE = MEANS STD CORR;

ANALYSIS:        ESTIMATOR = ML;
MODEL:           i s | A1@0 A2@1 A3;
                 i s ON P1 P2 P3 P4;
OUTPUT:          TECH1 TECH8 sampstat;

Here's the R code:

model_L <- ' i =~ 1*A1 + 1*A2 + 1*A3
               s =~ 0*A1 + 1*A2 + 2*A3

        # regressions der Kovariaten
          i ~ P1 + P2 + P3 + P4
          s ~ P1 + P2 + P3 + P4'

out <- growth.mi(model_L, data=mydata, miPackage="mice",
        miArgs=list(ords = c("P1, "P2")), m = 20, chi="all", mimic="Mplus")
summary(out, standardized=TRUE)

The findings regarding the significance of the predictors are consistent (the coefficients are not identical though).

2: In lavaan::lavaan(model = model_S, data = mydata, missing = "ML",  :
  lavaan WARNING: observed variable error term matrix (theta) is not positive definite; use inspect(fit,"theta") to investigate.

(I actually have the same problem with some other outcome variables as well).

I still get a reasonable output and the findings for the predictors are consistent with MPlus.

Now my questions are:
What does the plain intercept tell me, should we get the same results here?
What does the warning tell me, given that lavaan still computes reasonable estimates?
What could be the reason for the differing results (maybe the imputation?), and should I be concerned?

Thank you very much =)

Google groups seems to strip internet quotation marks when I use them, so I am inserting initials.

TG: Now my questions are:
What does the plain intercept tell me, should we get the same results here?

KM: The intercept (i) is the height of the curve at time zero.  You should only expect the same results to the extent that you analyze the same data.  Running the imputations separately means that you are analyzing different data.  A good strategy might be to share a set of imputed data sets and compare your results.  That would allow you to distinguish differences due to imputation from differences due to estimation.

TG: What does the warning tell me, given that lavaan still computes reasonable estimates?

KM: It may be that you are pushing the envelope with respect to sample size, proportion missing, or some other feature of your data that impacts estimation.  It may be that Mplus was more successful in producing start values.  You might try comparing lavaan and Mplus with the same user-specified start values.

TG: What could be the reason for the differing results (maybe the imputation?), and should I be concerned?

KM: Some possibilities:  (1) analyzing different data due to separate imputation, (2) different start values, (3) different estimated sampling error due to different imputation parameters, (2) different imputation models.

It is hard to answer whether you should be concerned because it is hard to discern the purpose behind the replication of the analysis.  Breaking the analysis into stages so that you can isolate where the differences occur may offer a useful strategy.

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Lavaan uses listwise deletion or FIML. This is explained in the documentation of the “missing” argument:

If "listwise", cases with missing values are removed listwise from the data frame before analysis. If "direct" or "ml" or "fiml" and the estimator is max- imum likelihood, Full Information Maximum Likelihood (FIML) estimation is used using all available data in the data frame. This is only valid if the data are missing completely at random (MCAR) or missing at random (MAR). If "default", the value is set depending on the estimator and the mimic option.

If you prefer to use multiple imputation, you can do that with the semTools package.

Mikko

Dear Heather, Yves, & lavaan users,

For my own analyses (I’m studying food web dynamics in California), I had a similar wish to include a random effect in my models.

My understanding is that it is possible to do so through the package lavaan.survey (Oberski D. 2014, see an introduction by the author to his package here: http://www.inside-r.org/packages/cran/lavaan.survey/docs/lavaan.survey). Yves advised so in 2012 in this discussion: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/lavaan/random$20effect/lavaan/3XhnM7CoaVU/JfqyOehlsyAJ. See also this more recent discussion: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/lavaan/random$20effect/lavaan/wjIKICrzHog/p6mLZCQ_M8YJ.

I won’t repeat here what is explained in the link provided above. However, to fully answer Heather original question, I’ll add a question regarding the exact use of lavaan.survey, in particular the step during which you describe your sampling design.

This involves the following code (as you can see following the above links):

       survey.design <- svydesign(ids=~your.block.column, prob=~1, data=your.dataset)

      #=> this would set Heather’s blocks as clusters.

However, the following is also feasible:

       survey.design <- svydesign(ids=~1, strata=~your.block.column, prob=~1, data=your.dataset)

      #=> this would set Heather’s blocks as stratum.

The issue is that, running my models with both options, the outcomes were very different. Using the “clusters” option increased a lot the fit between my model and my data. However, the fit between model and data slightly decreased when following the “stratum” option. This suggests that either option must be chosen in full understanding of its meaning and use in the model assessment.

Any help/clarification on how to choose between these options would be really helpful.

Cheers,

Nicolas

Well, this is your problem (the first of many): the sample covariance
matrix of your observed variables for the first group can not be
inverted. This means the covariance matrix is singular. Maybe, some
variables are a linear combination of other variables?

It would seem you have a fairly large model, and your sample size in
group 2 (N=205) is way too small to get a reliable estimate of the
weight matrix. Using non-normal corrections may not be feasible for your
sample.

messages.subject_clean: Meaning of Modification indices / EPC ?
messages.body_plain:
The Ms and EPCs apply to parameters whose estimated values are fixed or constrained.  The EPC estimates how much (and in what direction) the constrained estimate would move if the constraint were removed.  For a parameter estimate that is not constrained, both MI and EPC should be 0.  The MI gives you a test statistic (a lower bound, as compared to an actual chi-square difference statistic) while the EPC gives you a measure of practical relevance, or effect size.  As always, keep the scaling of variables in mind.  EPC could misleadingly appear to be 0 if one variable has a much larger variance than another.
--Ed Rigdon
